newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran president-elect says U.S. holds key to ties.
newsitem.headline: Iran president-elect says U.S. holds key to ties.

text.p: Iranian president-elect Mohammad Khatami said on Tuesday Washington and not Iran held the key to any thaw in the icy relations between the Islamic republic and the United States.
"The key of the problem is in their hands and not us," Khatami told his first news conference after winning a landslide victory in last Friday's polls.
"Our relations with the United States will depend on observing changes in their attitude towards us, but unfortunately we have not seen anything," said Khatami, a moderate former culture minister.
"We are sorry to see that the United States policy has always been...hostile to our revolution," he told Iranian and foreign journalists.

"We cannot accept domineering...policies. Any change in relations with the United States depends on changes in the policies of America towards the revolution and Iran, and unfortunately we do not see any sign of such change in American policy," said Khatami, speaking through an interpreter.
"In regard to relations with the United States of America, I should say that America is the source...of this problem," said the 54-year-old Khatami.
Khatami said "there will be no ground for any relations" between the two countries as long as the United States wanted to harm Iranian independence and national interest.

"The great outcome of our revolution is independence and we are not willing to give up this valuable outcome we have gained. The basis of our relations with other countries relies on the independence and national interest of our country," he said.

Iran has repeatedly denied U.S. accusations it supported international terrorism and was developing nuclear weapons. Iranian leaders had said any breakthrough in relations with the United States depended on a change in U.S. policy.

The United States -- which has imposed sanctions on Iran in an effort to isolate it -- has said it was closely watching the aftermath of Iran's elections to see if there were changes in the country's behaviour.
"We have always been against terrorism and especially state terrorism," said Khatami, who takes over his post as president in August.

Khatami's landslide election victory was the biggest political upset in Iran since the revolution. Iranian analysts and Western diplomats had forecast a close race but none predicted he would crush the establishment's candidate, parliamentary speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri.

Khatami is an Islamic intellectual remembered as a tolerant politician when he was culture minister for most of the 1980s. He replaces President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, who must step down after completing two four-year terms of office.
The presidency is revolutionary Iran's highest elective office but the country's supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, has paramount authority in setting domestic and foreign policy.
